subject: Nmix.gof.test() produces error related to K

messages.author: 77e0f8e9f257430f
messages.subject: Nmix.gof.test() produces error related to K
parts:
Hello, dear unmarked members! I am trying to run bootstraps for my most parsimonious models for 4 species (point count data on birds). However, my code produced an error.

#Check highest recorded frequency to choose a value for K. K should be higher
max(y, na.rm=TRUE)
#Gives output 6

#Fit the model
dm3 <-pcountOpen(~1, ~1, ~1, ~Cloud, data = umf, mixture = "ZIP", K = 100, dynamics = "autoreg", fix = "none", se = TRUE)

#Bootstrap to check goodness of fit
Nmix.gof.test(dm3, nsim = 10, plot.hist = TRUE, report = NULL, parallel = TRUE)

The last function produces this error:

Error in pcountOpen(lambdaformula = ~1, gammaformula = ~1, omegaformula = ~1,  : 
  specified K is too small. Try a value larger than any observation

How can K = 100 be too small, when my highest frequency for this species is 6? Input would be very much appreciated :)

messages.author: 4e956cc50ac3e075
messages.subject: RE: [unmarked] Nmix.gof.test() produces error related to K
parts:
Hi Krisztina,


When you look at the predicted values for the abundance in each year from your model, do you get high values and very low values of p? Remember that if your model produces high estimates of abundance, the data set simulated from the model will also have high abundance values (thus the warning message about K being too low). This would be a first thing to check with your original model.


Best,


Marc

parts:
Yes, even though the documentation says "This should be higher than the maximum observed count", in practice I realized it needs to be higher than N. Which can lead to issues when increased K also increases N (and lowers the AIC). This is written up in: 
Kery, Marc. 2018. “Identifiability in N-Mixture Models: a Large-Scale Screening Test with Bird Data.” Ecology 99 (2): 281–88. doi:10.1002/ecy.2093.

I ran into a similar issue and I ended up not going with my NB model because it wasn't stable, but P and ZIP models were (tested by increasing K and checking N and the AIC).

messages.author: 4a635fe980c8c1cd
messages.subject: Re: [unmarked] Nmix.gof.test() produces error related to K
parts: Just to chime in quickly, K and N--if N is the finite sample population size estimate derived by summing across all of the sites (I'm guessing it is here based on previous posts)--are separate things. The fitted model involves integrating over all possible values for each N_i (or N_i_t, for an open model)--K needs to be larger than any reasonable value for these. Exp(2.96) is about 20, and the population appears to be growing. In year two, you might expect (20*.88) survivors and 20*.15 recruits (i.e., something like 20.6 birds), so keep in mind that the expected value of N could be quite a bit larger if there are a lot of years, here.   E(N) could be also substantially larger than 20 for some sites * time-periods if there are some covariate effects that aren't being presented above.

messages.author: 4a635fe980c8c1cd
messages.subject: Re: [unmarked] Nmix.gof.test() produces error related to K
parts: For the record, K should be larger than any plausible value for N_i (or N_i,t), because K defines the upper limit for integration that occurs at the site (or site by year) level. As Geraldine suggested, increasing K could solve the bootstrap issue, or if your estimates never really stabilize as K increases, then there are deeper problems. My point was largely that one increases K on the basis of reasonable site-specific abundances, rather than the sum of abundances across sites.
Hello John, which equation are you using when you arrive at 20? Because when I run sum(bup()) I get a population of 248 for year 1. Maybe I am confusing myself here.

I was ball-parking the expected abundance using exp(lambda intercept), which I thought was 2.96: upon re-reading, the intercept is 1.08 and  2.96 = exp(1.08) = expected abundance. So to reiterate, the expected abundance at a a site (ignoring any variation) is about 3, (and not 20). You are summing estimates of the site-specific abundances.

Another problem I ran into is that I get different numbers for the population parameters depending on if i use the exp() and plogis() or if I just call the model and look at the output... So the numbers for lambda, gamma, etc. that I wrote above I got by running:
exp(coef(dm3_sky, type="lambda"))
exp(coef(dm3_sky, type="gamma"))
plogis(coef(dm3_sky, type="omega"))

But when I call my model dm3_sky I get
lambda= 1.08
gamma= -1.9
omega= 1.99

when you call the model, it returns coefficients on, say, the log or logit scale--this is a a convenient thing to do for fitting purposes. The actual values need to be backtransformed, which you've done with the plogis and exp calls.
